title: Decoding AI Labels: What ‘Open-Source’ Really Means for Models Like LLaMa and DeepSeek
summary: When you hear that an AI model is “open,” don’t picture a friendly chatbot. The label refers to accessibility: can developers see, modify, and share the model’s inner workings? The concept traces back to the free software movement of the 1980s, which championed four freedoms: run, study, redistribute, and improve. For decades, “open source” meant releasing the source code — the fundamental instructions. But with large language models, the definition has splintered. Take Meta’s LLaMa, released in February 2023. The company made the inference code and “weights” (the encoded knowledge from training) publicly available. Yet its license prohibits commercial reuse, which the Open Source Initiative (OSI) argues disqualifies it as truly open. This has given rise to the term “open-weight” — a middle ground where the trained parameters are shared, but the training data and sometimes full code remain proprietary. Other players have pushed further. DeepSeek and Alibaba’s Qwen released models with less restrictive terms, fueling rapid adoption in the AI community. Still, many developers insist that a genuinely open-source AI must include the training data — the vast datasets that teach the model. The OSI’s forthcoming definition makes this a requirement, but it raises practical concerns: distributing terabytes of data is logistically daunting. The stakes are high. Open models can democratize AI, allowing researchers and startups to innovate without permission from tech giants. But closed models, like OpenAI’s GPT series, offer tighter control and potentially more polished products. As the debate rages, one thing is clear: the label on the tin doesn’t always match what’s inside. Understanding the difference between closed, open-weight, and fully open-source AI is crucial for anyone navigating this rapidly evolving landscape.
why_it_matters: As artificial intelligence becomes woven into daily life, knowing whether a model is truly open matters for fairness and innovation. A generation of future coders and users must be able to see through marketing labels to understand who controls the technology and what they can do with it — ultimately shaping whether AI serves the many or the few.

background_read: The term 'open source' was first applied to software in the late 1990s, building on the earlier 'free software' movement led by programmer Richard Stallman. That movement championed four freedoms: the right to run, study, redistribute, and improve code.

The Open Source Initiative (OSI), a non-profit that certifies software licenses, created a 10-point definition to distinguish truly open programs from proprietary ones. AI models are more complex than traditional software: they include not just code but also 'weights' (the numerical patterns learnt from data) and massive training datasets.

When Meta (the parent company of Facebook and Instagram) released LLaMa in 2023, it made the weights and some code available but used a restrictive license — sparking debate over whether the model qualified as open source. Meanwhile, Chinese companies DeepSeek and Alibaba's Qwen released models with less restrictive terms, fuelling rapid adoption.

The push to include training data in the definition of open-source AI raises practical problems: distributing terabytes of data is logistically difficult and expensive, and some datasets contain copyrighted or personal information.

perspectives.description: Open-weight models lower barriers for researchers, students, and startups who cannot afford closed AI services. They enable more transparency, allowing users to inspect and customize the technology, which can lead to breakthroughs in fields like medicine, education, and local language tools in under-resourced communities.

Fully open models, especially when training data is included, could be misused to generate disinformation, hate speech, or harmful instructions. Companies argue that keeping some components closed helps prevent malicious actors from exploiting the AI, and that proprietary control ensures better safety monitoring and quality assurance.

The debate mirrors past battles in software — like the rise of Linux versus Windows — where the balance between openness and commercial viability reshaped entire industries. With AI, the stakes are higher because the technology can influence elections, economies, and personal privacy; the definition of 'open' is not just technical but deeply political and ethical.

As the Open Source Initiative finalizes its AI definition, governments and international bodies may adopt similar criteria for regulation. The outcome will influence whether the next wave of AI is built by a handful of tech giants or by a diverse global community. Future users will need literacy in these labels to make informed choices about the tools they trust.
